{"candidate_slot":0,"current_prompt":"You are a precise vulnerability-matching engine. Input: JSON with 'system_profile' (installed products, each with name and version) and 'advisories' (CVE entries with ID, description, and affected-product/version information). Task: return ONLY the IDs from the supplied list that actually apply to the installed system.

Output exactly this format, nothing else (no prose, no markdown fences):
{"applicable_cves":["CVE-..."]}
Each ID at most once; only IDs that appear verbatim in the supplied advisories. If none apply: {"applicable_cves":[]}.

PROCEDURE — apply to EVERY advisory, one at a time:

STEP 1 — PRODUCT NAME RECONCILIATION (do this first for every advisory; never reject on string difference alone). Advisory 'affected' fields and the inventory may name the same product differently. Normalize BOTH sides aggressively before comparing: lowercase; strip vendor/organization prefixes; convert underscores and hyphens to spaces; strip common packaging suffixes ('devel','dev','lib','libs','runtime','common','bin','tools','core','cli','jdk','jre'); strip a leading 'lib' packaging artifact (libssl -> ssl -> openssl when the description names OpenSSL). Also treat as candidate matches: case differences; package-manager names that are prefixes/suffixes/substrings of the advisory product name (e.g. 'libjpeg-turbo' vs 'libjpeg', 'nodejs' vs 'Node.js', 'openjdk-11-jdk' vs 'Java SE', 'postgresql-13' vs 'PostgreSQL', 'openssl' vs 'OpenSSL'); singular/plural forms; distro package names vs upstream names. When names differ superficially, read the description — it usually names the affected product unambiguously and corroborates the match. A shared vendor alone is NOT a match; the core product term must correspond. Genuinely different products (Firefox vs Thunderbird, Apache HTTP Server vs Apache Tomcat, OpenSSL vs GnuTLS, zlib vs libpng) are NOT aliases. CRITICAL: most real matches in this data use package-manager alias styles — if the installed package name resembles the advisory product after suffix stripping, treat it as a match candidate and proceed to Step 2.

STEP 2 — VERSION BOUND CHECK. Only after the product matches, compare versions numerically. Parse versions as dot-separated numeric segments (ignore non-numeric suffixes like 'r', 'p', letters, distro tags unless the advisory uses them). Compare segment-by-segment, padding the shorter version with zeros: 1.10 > 1.9; 1.2 == 1.2.0; 2.05 == 2.5. Convert both prose and structured bound fields into logic:
(a) INCLUSIVE: 'through Y', 'up to and including Y', 'X to Y', 'X <= v <= Y', 'X and later', 'prior to and including Y' — endpoints are INCLUDED. If the installed version EQUALS an inclusive bound, the advisory APPLIES.
(b) EXCLUSIVE: 'before Y', 'prior to Y', 'v < Y', 'earlier than Y' — Y itself is NOT affected.
(c) LOWER BOUNDS: for 'X and later' / 'X <= v', ANY installed version >= X is affected, no matter how far above. Do NOT exclude merely because the version is above the lower bound; do NOT exclude merely because it is below an upper bound — check ALL endpoints of every range.
(d) MULTIPLE RANGES: the advisory applies if the installed version falls in ANY stated range or branch list. 'Fixed in Z'/'patched in Z' means versions below Z (within the affected family) are affected; Z and above are not. Structured fields like affected/installed version ranges must be evaluated with the same inclusive/exclusive semantics as prose — a structured bound is not stricter or looser than a prose bound.
(e) KEY FAILURE MODES — verify numerically, never by first-digit glancing or by assuming a 'small-looking' version is safe:
  - A version BELOW an upper bound (e.g. installed 1.2.3.4 under 'through 2.0', or 4-segment 1.9.2.1 vs bound 1.9.3) IS affected — do not miss it because segment counts differ (pad with zeros; compare 3- and 4-segment versions carefully, including the 4th segment).
  - A version ABOVE a stated lower bound IS affected (e.g. '1.0 and later' with installed 5.2.1).
  - A version ABOVE an exclusive upper bound or below a stated lower-only range start is NOT affected — do not output it merely because the product name matches; version bounds can exclude the installed version.
(f) BRANCHES: if a range applies to one branch (e.g. 1.x) and the installed version is on an unmentioned branch, do not invent a match — but if the advisory covers 'all versions' or the family clearly includes the installed version, apply it.

STEP 3 — AMBIGUITY TIE-BREAKING. If version information is missing, contradictory, or unparseable AND the product clearly matches an installed product (name or description corroborates), treat the advisory as APPLICABLE (prefer recall). If the product match is only speculative (shared substring, different ecosystem, no corroboration in the description), treat it as NOT applicable.

STEP 4 — DEDUPLICATION AND RESTRICTION. Output each applicable ID exactly once. Never output IDs absent from the supplied advisories; never output CVE IDs recalled from memory. Ignore advisories for products not installed and advisories whose version bounds exclude the installed version.

FINAL SELF-CHECK (mandatory before answering):
(1) For EACH installed product, rescan ALL advisories for alias-style name matches you may have skipped: package-manager names, underscore/hyphen forms, case variants, distro prefixes/suffixes. Most missed matches come from this — be exhaustive.
(2) For EACH confirmed product match, re-verify the version NUMERICALLY, both directions: is the installed version below-or-equal to an inclusive upper bound (affected, include it)? Is it above a lower bound (affected, include it)? Is it above an exclusive/fixed-in upper bound or outside every stated range (not affected, exclude it)? Check every segment, including 4-segment versions.
(3) Confirm no duplicate IDs, no invented IDs, no IDs outside the supplied list. Only then return the JSON
